newsitem.title: USA: Opening of Oklahoma case moves some to tears.
newsitem.headline: Opening of Oklahoma case moves some to tears.

text.p: Heart-wrenching images painted on Thursday in the Oklahoma City bombing case reduced some survivors and victims' families to tears as those closest to the 168 people who died began the ordeal of watching the trial of Timothy McVeigh.

"It was very emotional, there were some tears and some of us choked up," said Paul Heath, a Veterans Administration psychologist who survived the April 19, 1995, explosion, after the opening statements in the trial.
Some of the saddest words came from chief prosecutor Joseph Hartzler as he described the last minutes in the lives of the children who died in the Alfred P. Murrah federal building.
One toddler was just comforting a friend who was crying as his mother left him in the building's daycare centre, he said.
The opening gambit by defence attorney Stephen Jones featured a slow and sombre reading of the names of each of the 168 people who perished.
As the names were read aloud, Tom Kight put his arm around his wife Marsha, whose 23-year-old daughter was killed.
"I don't think it's intended to hurt us. That's his job," Heath said outside the courtroom, adding that he was steeled for a difficult time ahead. "I'm all right. I'll be fine."

About 14 bombing survivors and victims' family members attended the opening day of arguments in the crowded Denver courtroom. Some, like Heath, arrived at 5:30 a.m. amid a heavy snowstorm to get a seat. Kight, who has attended most of the pretrial proceedings, said she was "entirely exhausted."
Sitting just a few feet away was the tall, thin, crewcut McVeigh, wore an open-necked casual blue plaid shirt and khaki trousers. His face was pale after his two years in prison.
He looked serious and appeared to listen closely as the prosecutor described him as an extremist, hate-filled man who hatched the bombing plot, built the deadly device and finally set it off.

McVeigh furrowed his brow once in a while, especially when the prosecutor would offer a particularly minute detail, such as a recognisable 'curly-q' in McVeigh's handwriting or proof of the times he allegedly made damning telephone calls.

He smiled only once during the morning court session, when U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch ordered the jurors not take notes, even though everyone else in the courtroom could. McVeigh had busily scribbled notes and messages to his defence team throughout the pretrial legal proceedings.
The mood overall in the courtroom was one of respectful silence, a demeanor Heath said "would make any American proud."

One light moment came when Hartzler arrived at the courthouse in the heavy wet snow, singing softly, "Oh, what a beautiful morning. Oh, what a beautiful day," the well-known lyrics from the musical "Oklahoma."
